title: Boron in Plants: What It Does and When Your Crop Needs It
metaTitle: Boron in Plants: Role, Signs and When It Matters
metaDescription: Boron in plants builds cell walls and makes pollen work. See why fruit and seed crops need it at flowering, and why too much is close to enough.
excerpt: Boron in plants helps build cell walls and makes pollen grow, so flowers turn into fruit and seed. It does not move to new growth, so a shortage hits the growing tips and the flowers first. Fruit crops, root crops and coconut need it most. Here is what it does, when each crop needs it, and why the gap between enough and too much is small.

heroImage.alt: Coconut frond with leaflets stuck together and crumpled: boron in plants running short

blocks.text:
Boron ties together the pieces of the cell wall, so new cells form strong and whole. It also helps sugar move through the plant and keeps the growing tips dividing.

Its biggest job comes at flowering. Pollen needs boron to grow its tube down to the ovule, so a crop short of boron flowers but sets little fruit or seed. That is why boron shows up as hollow stems in broccoli, cracked roots in carrot, poorly filled ears in mais and button nuts in coconut.
A building block in tiny amounts

Boron is a building block of the cell wall, though it is needed only in grams per hectare. Once laid down it stays where it is, much like calcium, so the plant cannot move it to new leaves or flowers.

That makes boron a nutrient of steady supply. The crop needs a little all the time, and above all at flowering, rather than a big dose once.

blocks.caption: Boron in short
rows: The growing tips, young leaves and flowers

blocks.text:
Because boron hardly moves, the shortage starts at the growing points. Tips die back, young leaves come out thick, brittle or crumpled, flowers drop and fruit crack or grow hollow.

See [boron deficiency](/nutrient-deficiencies/boron-deficiency) for the signs in each crop.
When boron in plants is most critical

Boron matters most from flowering to fruit set, and in root crops and cabbage while the root or head forms. Palay needs very little.

DAT means days after transplanting, DAS days after sowing in the field, and DAP days after planting. The days are the usual ones for a typical variety, so a long or short variety moves them a little. Timing boron in plants to these windows gets more harvest from the same bags. Our guide to [fertilizer timing by growth stage](/blog/fertilizer-timing-by-growth-stage) puts them together for a whole season.

blocks.text: What keeps boron from the crop

Boron washes out of sandy soil and soil low in organic matter in heavy rain. Liming acid soil past neutral also makes it harder to take up, and a dry spell stops its flow into the plant.

So the risk is highest on light, limed or upland soils in a wet season followed by a dry spell at flowering.

Borax and solubor are the usual sources, on the soil or as a weak spray before flowering. Many foliar fertilizers carry a little boron. See [foliar fertilizer](/blog/foliar-fertilizer) and [fertilizer for vegetables](/blog/fertilizer-for-vegetables-philippines).

items: Borax: on the soil, mixed evenly with other fertilizer.
Solubor (sodium borate): dissolves fast, for leaf sprays.

blocks.title: The line between enough and too much is thin
blocks.text: Boron burns leaf edges and kills young plants at only a few times the right rate. Spread it evenly, never pile it, and follow the label to the gram.

blocks.title: Have boron in place before the flowers open
blocks.text: Put your fertilizers on your crop's calendar in anee.io and the [Coverage Planner](/features/residual-effect-calendar) shows, day by day, whether boron reaches the stages that need it, and where it runs out. Free to start.
blocks.label: Start free

items.a: Before flowering, so it is there when the pollen grows. On fruit crops a light spray at the start of flowering is common.

items.q: What does boron deficiency look like?
items.a: Dead or crumpled growing tips, brittle young leaves, flowers that drop, and fruit or roots that crack or grow hollow.
In very small amounts it supplies boron. A little too much harms the crop, so measure carefully and spread it evenly.
Very little. Most rice soils give enough, and too much boron is the more common trouble in rice.
